So listen, during this episode, you're going to learn why inflation is a terrible benchmark for freight budgets, how tariffs, duty responsibility can dramatically change your exposure and what accessorials really are. specifically how they can turn a manageable shipment into a massive cost spike. ICC has been around a lot longer than me. ICC started in 1975. The founder, Tony Muzio, used to be in the logistics industry as a traffic manager. And the frustrations of doing that work kind of led to the creation of ICC. As a traffic manager, you're auditing bills, analyzing contracts, doing routing design, and making sure everything's being tendered properly. And Tony realized that he could help companies do this better from being an impartial extension of their logistics team to come in and bring good processes to optimize transportation and logistics operations. Would you say that that is the main thing that your company does? I mean, the foundation is for us, I always like to say there's no Bloomberg for freight. So it teaches you to be forensic. And yes, auditing is forensic for things like how is the service? Was it on time? Is the rate correct? Is the cost competitive? Is the design of the supply chain execution efficient? Those are all things that we audit. And they are different challenges for each type of company. Some companies just ship to their customers. Or some bring in supplies from China and then distribute it to various warehouses where it gets more manufacturing before it's ready to be shipped out. So auditing is at the core of what we do, and it leads to all of the benefits with contract optimization, benchmarking insights. Again, there's no Bloomberg for freight. So big, medium, small. Shippers only see what's inside their data. They don't know what anyone else proprietarily negotiated. And those insights are valuable for freight. So I think that's really important as we pivot to this next part of this conversation. And I want to talk about the markets a little bit. As inflation continues to run above 2%, there has been talk about odds of another rate hike. What does that mean for transportation budgets over the next two quarters, particularly for companies that assume their freight costs would eventually stabilize? pending_qa.q: How can companies validate tariff classifications to avoid unnecessary cost penalties?
pending_qa.r: Companies must ensure their HTS codes are proper and that all descriptions and labeling are in good order, as tariffs can be more expensive when incorrect shipping information is provided. When tariffs are valid and applied correctly, auditing is the due diligence to ensure proper billing. Companies should also look at importer of record responsibilities and examine whether changing INCO terms could relieve tariff obligations. Oliver Najumi notes that when auditing, ICC finds significant money in customers and brokers not communicating correct classification codes, resulting in higher tariff costs or penalties from customs.

pending_qa.q: What are accessorial charges and how dramatically can they impact total shipping costs?
pending_qa.r: Accessorials are simply surcharges applied to freight, fuel, and other shipping components. In small package shipping, they can be much more impactful. One furniture customer spending $400,000 annually has 47% of their costs as accessorials. For instance, an accessorial charge for items over 48 inches in length or over 40 pounds increased from $9 in 2015 to $58.75 today, a 582% increase in 11 years. The application of these surcharges changes quietly over time, and when thresholds shift, exposure can increase dramatically—one customer's costs jumped $200,000 annually when weight and dimension measurements were adjusted.

pending_qa.q: How should CFOs distinguish between legitimate cost increases and billing leakage in freight expenses?
pending_qa.r: Legitimate cost increases, such as correctly billed and owed tariffs, are not leakage—they are just increased costs to do business. Actual leakage shows up in missed billings, improperly applied charges, and inefficient routing. It can result from warehouses not measuring and weighing things correctly, causing higher billing than what is manifested. The real risk occurs when tariffs, inflation, and carrier prices all rise simultaneously while billing errors become indistinguishable, causing CFOs to miss significant leakage and accept 15% increases without auditing. Companies should analyze shipment profiles, routing efficiency, and actual carrier pricing to identify where leakage occurs.

pending_qa.q: What specific process should a logistics leader follow when brought in to protect freight margin over a 90-day period?
pending_qa.r: First, pull the most recent trailing 12 months of all data to understand the specific shipper's actual shipment profile and exposures. Then organize internal routing principles to understand how the portfolio of logistics providers is executed logically. After that, run this data against a data warehouse containing roughly $9 billion a year of shipping cost transactional data to see what is competitive and what is not. Oliver Najumi emphasizes showing folks what works with real actual pricing, not idealistic scenarios, to formulate a realistic solution. This entire process takes about two weeks and creates a moving target budget that adjusts as market conditions change, rather than a fixed budget that may become severely outdated.

pending_qa.q: When does carrier diversification beyond a primary carrier like UPS actually create financial leverage versus added operational complexity?
pending_qa.r: Carrier diversification creates leverage and flexibility by reducing single-carrier dependency and mitigating catastrophic network disruptions, such as cyber attacks or air disasters. In one case, a customer spending $5 million with UPS could save up to $1.6 million annually (50% savings) by moving 30% of low-weight shipment volume to an alternative carrier. A more established alternative carrier offered 33% savings. Implementation should be gradual through a testing model—starting with a small volume allocation, validating billing and system integration, then increasing volume step by step. This approach allows companies to remain open to additional carriers if they make sense, while maintaining service quality and reducing risk.

pending_qa.q: How can AI tools assist in freight contract review and invoice auditing while avoiding common pitfalls?
pending_qa.r: AI is strong at anomaly detection in data warehouses when trained correctly with proper mathematical boundaries, reading contract and service guide language to extract and flag inconsistencies across hundreds of thousands of invoice lines. However, AI does not replace human analysis and makes consistent mistakes. It does not bring outside benchmark data, so comparing internal data through AI only shows the same mirror faster. Many shippers misuse AI by throwing out egregiously wild negotiation targets with no defensible logic. Oliver Najumi cautions that AI should be a tool to enhance and validate, not a replacement for proper freight auditing and benchmarking.

pending_qa.q: What is the most universally understandable key performance indicator for freight cost management that CFOs can digest without daily shipping expertise?
pending_qa.r: Cost per pound, aligned with freight classification and service level assigned to the shipment, is the most digestible and defensible measure for C-level executives. Whether managing one carrier in one mode or 22 carriers across various modes, cost per pound consistently proves to be the metric that C-level individuals understand. While other KPIs may be better for specific niches, the goal when presenting to executives who are not in shipping daily is to make the data simple and comprehensible—like two plus two equals four.

pending_qa.q: What is the most widely overestimated need in modern parcel shipping strategy?
pending_qa.r: The overuse of express shipping is a widely accepted logistics practice that is overdue for retirement. Many companies use express shipping more than necessary when ground shipping offers comparable service and delivery times at a fraction of the cost. While influenced by Amazon-driven customer expectations of immediate delivery, modeling different scenarios can reveal significant savings without negotiating rates. This requires supply chain redesign, but the cost-benefit analysis of switching from express to ground is often favorable.
